newsitem.title: USA: Federal trial opens this week for Arizona governor.
newsitem.headline: Federal trial opens this week for Arizona governor.

text.p: Embattled Arizona Gov. Fife Symington goes on trial in U.S. District Court Tuesday, facing fraud, extortion and perjury charges that could end his career and send him to prison.
Some say that Arizona's reputation also will be on trial when jury selection begins before Federal Judge Roger Strand.

Inside Courtroom 8, Symington, a colourful, 51-year-old Republican, will begin his defence against 22 felony charges. Federal prosecutors will try to prove to a jury that Symington committed fraud, extortion and perjury in connection with real estate deals during the last decade.
If convicted on even a single count, the two-term governor will be booted from the office he has held since 1991. He also faces a possible prison term.

"We're ready for the trial to get under way," David Schindler, an assistant U.S. attorney, said. "It's certainly a complicated case ... but it's really not much different than any other fraud case that we prosecute."

Prosecutors will detail what they claim are deliberate lies told by Symington from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, when he was a prominent developer, to secure credit lines and business and personal loans.

The government contends that Symington made false statements to lenders to prevent his real estate empire from crumbling. Prosecutors also will try to prove that Symington extorted an agreement from six union pension funds to release him from a personal loan guarantee he made to obtain a $10 million loan for a shopping centre in downtown Phoenix.
Last, the government will try to prove that the governor lied under oath during court proceedings when he filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September 1995.
"We wouldn't be prosecuting if we didn't believe the evidence was there," Schindler said. "It's definitely there."

John Dowd, Symington's attorney, said he was anxious to prove his client's innocence. "It's always nice to get to the end of the road," he said. "We're on an even playing field now, and that's all we've wanted all along."
Dowd said it had not been decided whether Symington would testify. He declined to comment on the specifics of his defence, citing a gag order issued by the court.
The charges stem from a probe into the 1989 collapse of Southwest Savings & Loan Association. Symington served on the thrift's board of directors.

After settling the case, the U.S. Attorney's office in Los Angeles continued its probe into the governor's financial dealings for several years. Last June Symington was indicted in a move that drew national attention.
Since then, there have been calls for his resignation by the state's largest newspapers, and his popularity in public opinion polls has slipped to 30 percent.
Symington, a descendent of industrialist Henry Clay Frick, has repeatedly maintained his innocence and has said he plans to seek re-election in 1998.
Bruce Merrill, a professor of mass communications at Arizona State University, said the upcoming trial would be bad for the state regardless of what happened.

Merrill said coverage in the national press would further tarnish the image of Arizona, which already has a reputation for being a hotbed of militias and politicians of ill repute. A former governor, Evan Mecham, was indicted by a county grand jury in 1988 on criminal charges involving campaign financing. He was later acquitted but then impeached by the state legislature.

"It's going to continue the myth that we're just a state with a bunch of lunatics and wackos," said Merrill, a pollster and veteran political observer. "I can see it now. ... It can't help but hurt the state."
